    sandtablR

    A framework for mass-casualty incident tabletop exercise simulation, decision-path analysis and machine learning, with an interactive Shiny workbench.

    Generate a casualty cohort, run it across a board, capture the decisions that were made, then model and explain them.

    Installation 

    # install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("cttir/sandtablR")

    R 4.1.0 or later is required. The core installation includes the simulation and plotting dependencies. Modelling, explanations and sequence clustering have optional dependencies; install the ones needed for your workflow.

    Development software. Synthetic examples demonstrate interfaces and modelling assumptions. They do not establish clinical validity or real-world performance.

    Quick start 

    library(sandtablR)
co <- sdt_synthetic_cohort(n = 40, seed = 1)
sc <- sdt_scenario(co, resources = list(or = 3, icu_imc = 6, ward = 20))
run <- sdt_simulate(sc, replications = 5, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
summary(run, reference = TRUE)
head(sdt_decision_paths(run))
head(sdt_decision_consistency(run))

    The event log records patient movement by replication and board area. Summaries compare the simulated end state with a reference distribution; the comparison is not an independent clinical validation. Seeds make this example repeatable within the recorded software environment.

    For a small optional modelling example, install the listed dependencies first:

    # install.packages(c("parsnip", "recipes", "workflows", "rsample", "tune",
#                    "yardstick", "dials", "hardhat", "rpart"))
labelled <- sdt_add_decisions(co, seed = 2)
fit <- sdt_fit(labelled, target = "called_triage", engine = "tree",
               tune = FALSE, folds = 3, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
sdt_metrics(fit)

    Launch the interactive workbench separately:

    # Install the suggested Shiny dependencies listed in DESCRIPTION if needed.
sdt_run_app()

    What is in it

    A data model. A casualty is a patient card; an ordered set of them is a cohort; a cohort plus board capacities is a scenario. Cohort validation is vectorised over columns, so a bad import names every offending row and column at once instead of aborting on the first.

    A simulation engine. A discrete-event model over the board, routing each casualty by sighting category and therapy concept. It records a per-area event log, which is what makes full decision paths available downstream. The default horizon and board capacities were calibrated so the end-of-game distribution reproduces the published one; sdt_reference_scenario() builds that board, and the test suite re-runs the comparison rather than asserting it.

    Decision-path analysis. Pathways as state sequences, with optimal-matching distances, clustering into characteristic routes, and consistency scored as distance between a casualty’s replications rather than agreement on one label.

    A model bench. One interface over interpretable engines (glmnet, a decision tree) and black-box ones (ranger, xgboost), all trained through the same recipe and scored on the same held-out split, so performance can be compared under the same evaluation design.

    Explainability. Permutation importance, dependence profiles and per-casualty SHAP attributions via DALEX, all model-agnostic, so a tree and a forest can be compared on one footing.

    A workbench. Seven panels covering the whole workflow, plus a one-click self-contained HTML report of the session. The app’s modules are ordinary package functions in R/, not scripts under inst/, so they are checked, linted, covered and driven headlessly by the test suite.

    A note on what to predict

    The card’s true sighting category follows from life points by construction, so every engine scores near 1 on it and a leaderboard says nothing. What is worth modelling is what a participant called. sdt_add_decisions() generates those calls using the published per-category hit rates (88% red, 59% yellow, 71% green), which turns the bench into a real comparison. See vignette("model-bench").

    Authors

    Raban Heller and Gerhard Achatz.

    Provenance

    The domain model follows the TDSC tabletop exercise (Achatz et al. 2023, Eur J Trauma Emerg Surg 49(2):607–617, doi:10.1007/s00068-022-02217-1). sandtablR is a generic re-implementation built from the published specification and general knowledge. It is not TDSC course software and reproduces none of the course’s materials. G. Achatz is a developer of the TDSC course and an author of the evaluation the package calibrates against.

    sdt_reference() keeps the values attributed to that publication separate from sandtablR’s own modelling choices, so a calibration test cannot quietly check the model against parameters we picked ourselves.

    Tutorials and reproducibility

    • Getting started: cohort validation, simulation, decision paths, model fitting and saving results.
    • The model bench: a fixed, reproducible comparison of selected engines and the limits of model explanations.

    Install with remotes::install_github("CTTIR/sandtablR", build_vignettes = TRUE) to use vignette("sandtablR", package = "sandtablR") and vignette("model-bench", package = "sandtablR"). Building tutorials requires knitr, rmarkdown and Pandoc; optional modelling dependencies enable the corresponding tutorial sections.

    path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(list(scenario = sc, run = run, seed = 1,
             session = sessionInfo()), path)
restored <- readRDS(path)
stopifnot(identical(run$events, restored$run$events))

    Keep the scenario, seeds, package revision and software environment together. Synthetic data derived from real records are not automatically anonymous or safe to release. Assess privacy separately from predictive utility.

    Troubleshooting, citation and licence

    Validation errors identify invalid card fields; consult ?sdt_cohort for the schema. Optional-engine errors name the missing dependency. Start with the core simulation before adding modelling or explanation packages.

    Use citation("sandtablR") for installed-version metadata and cite the reference publication when using its attributed values. Licensed under MIT. Report reproducible problems with synthetic inputs in GitHub issues.
